Gastroenterology · published research

Radiation-induced enteropathy

PBM-preconditioned mesenchymal stem cells improved several intestinal tissue outcomes in one irradiated-mouse study. The experiment did not test PBM applied directly to the intestine or in patients.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

PBM-preconditioned mesenchymal stem cells improved several intestinal tissue outcomes in one irradiated-mouse study. The experiment did not test PBM applied directly to the intestine or in patients.

Summary of the Evidence

One 2019 publication combined cell-culture experiments using human umbilical-cord-blood mesenchymal stem cells with a mouse model of radiation-induced enteropathy. PBM was used to precondition the stem cells before they were administered. The irradiated intestine itself was not directly illuminated. The cell and mouse findings are two parts of one experimental programme, not separate clinical or independent animal studies.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study in people receiving abdominal radiotherapy was identified. Although some laboratory work used human-derived cells, that is cell-culture evidence and does not show how patients respond to treatment.

Animal evidence

After whole-abdominal X-ray irradiation, mice received PBM-preconditioned stem cells, untreated stem cells, or vehicle. The PBM-preconditioned-cell group had less mucosal destruction, better crypt-cell proliferation and epithelial-barrier measures, less loss of intestinal microvascular endothelial cells, and more angiogenesis in the lamina propria. These are favorable tissue outcomes in an acute radiation-injury model. The treatment was intravenous cell delivery after irradiation, not direct light exposure of the bowel (Kim et al. 2019).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In cultured human stem cells, 633-nm red visible light at 1 J/cm² increased cell proliferation and self-renewal. Conditioned medium from treated cells reduced radiation-related endothelial-cell apoptosis and loss of tube formation, alongside higher levels of angiogenic factors. These results support the cell-conditioning explanation tested in mice, but do not demonstrate an effect of PBM alone on intestinal tissue.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The cell experiments used 633-nm red light, with 1 J/cm² and an irradiance of 7.12 mW/cm² selected for the main experiments. In mice, the abdomen received 13.5 Gy of X-rays and the cell preparations were injected intravenously twice, two days apart. The study did not compare clinical routes, PBM-only treatment, or a range of cell-conditioning doses. The tested approach therefore concerns a combined cell-and-light strategy.

Interpretation

The publication reports improved intestinal barrier, crypt, endothelial, and angiogenesis measures after PBM-preconditioned cells were transplanted into irradiated mice. It supports a preclinical cell-conditioning strategy, but does not establish that PBM alone treats radiation enteropathy or improves outcomes for patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for PBM-preconditioned cell therapy in an irradiated mouse model
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One publication found improved intestinal tissue measures after mice received PBM-preconditioned stem cells. Light was applied to the cells before transplantation, not directly to the intestine, and no patient study was identified. Independent animal replication and studies separating the effects of cell transplantation from light preconditioning are needed before confidence can rise.
